channel.title: Daily Recap — 🚀 Space News
channel.description: What happened in 🚀 Space News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline at once
item.description:
Two of NASA's veteran Mars spacecraft hit trouble at the same time, taking half of the agency's aging fleet at the Red Planet out of action. The Perseverance rover is struggling to transmit data back to Earth, while the Mars Odyssey orbiter — in service since 2001 — is burning through its dwindling fuel supply at an alarming rate.

The simultaneous failures are a stark reminder of how much of NASA's Mars exploration now depends on hardware well past its design life. Perseverance is the centerpiece of the ongoing sample-collection campaign, and Odyssey serves as a key communications relay for surface missions. How much capability can be recovered — and how quickly — will shape the near-term outlook for science at Mars.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues

item.title: White House seeks $2 billion boost to accelerate Artemis
item.description:
The White House is pushing for a roughly $2 billion funding increase for NASA aimed at speeding up the Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon. Without the additional money, agency activities would face delays, underscoring how tight the program's schedule and budget already are.

The request signals that the administration sees the lunar timeline as a priority worth extra investment rather than a program to stretch out. The funding would still need congressional approval, so the proposal is the opening move in a budget fight — but it puts real money behind the push to keep Artemis moving faster.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis

item.title: Amazon turns to SpaceX and Ariane 6 after ULA fails to deliver Kuiper launches
item.description:
Amazon has hundreds of its Kuiper broadband satellites sitting in storage waiting for rides to orbit, and its original launch provider, United Launch Alliance, has failed to deliver the flights it promised. So Amazon has pivoted to the competition: its satellites are now flying on SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Europe's Ariane 6.

The shift is a telling sign of how the launch market has consolidated around a few reliable workhorses. ULA's delays have left Amazon scrambling to meet its deployment deadlines for the Kuiper constellation, while SpaceX — a direct rival in satellite broadband through Starlink — is now launching its competitor's satellites because it is the provider that can actually fly.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can

item.title: NASA locks in design for nuclear-powered SR-1 Freedom Mars mission
item.description:
NASA has completed a major design review for SR-1 Freedom, its first spacecraft powered by a nuclear fission reactor, and locked in key elements of the mission architecture. The spacecraft is targeted to launch in late 2028 and would demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.

SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall, a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once there, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history and search for signs of subsurface ice. A shorter reactor boom and improved shielding simplify the design, and NASA awarded Johns Hopkins APL a $39.3 million contract for the nuclear power module's heat rejection system. If it works, the technology could power future long-duration missions and lunar surface bases.

Sources

  • NASA: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom

item.title: Dragonfly gets its eyes as cameras arrive for Titan mission
item.description:
The science instruments for NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft are starting to arrive at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, where the car-sized craft is being assembled for its flight to Saturn's moon Titan. First to check in: DragonCam, a suite of seven cameras built by Malin Space Science Systems, now installed, tested, and integrated into the rotorcraft.

DragonCam will photograph Titan's surface at multiple scales, both in flight and on the ground, using a configurable LED array that can illuminate the surface in wavelengths from infrared to ultraviolet — letting scientists see Titan's terrain as human eyes would, and possibly spot organic molecules that fluoresce under UV light. The cameras will also guide sampling decisions for the mission's drill. Dragonfly is scheduled to launch in July 2028 and reach Titan in late 2034.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes

item.title: Cygnus XL to haul 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the space station
item.description:
NASA's Northrop Grumman CRS-25 resupply mission will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. It will be the third flight of the larger Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft, launching aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral.

The cargo includes experiments with real payoffs on Earth: a muscle-loss study testing whether existing FDA-approved drugs can slow atrophy, a microgravity manufacturing test for DNA-inspired drug-delivery particles, a tumor-replica investigation aimed at predicting cancer spread, a new radiation sensor for future Artemis missions, and a mostly automated plant-growth facility for long-duration spaceflight. After arrival, station astronauts will grapple the spacecraft with Canadarm2 and berth it to the Unity module for unloading.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview

item.title: Webb reveals hot dust in supernova remnant Cassiopeia A
item.description:
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has produced a high-resolution mid-infrared view of Cassiopeia A, revealing the hot dust left behind by the explosion of a massive star. The image, released November 23, shows the remnant in striking new detail.

Supernova remnants like Cas A are the clouds of gas and dust that eventually seed new generations of stars — and Webb's infrared vision lets astronomers trace the dust in ways earlier telescopes could not. It's a vivid reminder of the telescope's ongoing science output as it continues to re-image familiar objects with unprecedented clarity.

Sources

  • NASA: Webb Reveals New Details in Supernova Remnant

item.title: Reports: Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite as soon as next month
item.description:
Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear weapon into orbit far sooner than previously believed, with reports suggesting it could happen as early as next month. The prospect has alarmed space and security experts because a nuclear detonation in orbit would not be a contained event: the resulting radiation and electromagnetic effects could rapidly degrade or destroy thousands of satellites, crippling communications, navigation, weather forecasting, and military systems that modern life depends on.

Such a deployment would also shatter long-standing norms against placing weapons of mass destruction in space. The reports come amid already strained relations, and the timeline — weeks rather than years — leaves little room for diplomatic pushback. Watch for official responses from the U.S. government and allies, which will signal how seriously the intelligence is being taken and whether any countermeasures are on the table.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Reports: Russia may launch nuclear weapon into orbit as soon as next month

item.title: NASA seeks industry partners for the Moon's first nuclear reactor
item.description:
NASA is looking for industry partners to design and test the first nuclear reactor built to generate electricity on the Moon. The system, called Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), is a small fission power plant that would produce 20 kilowatts — enough to power roughly 16 homes — and serve as the backbone for a sustained human presence on the lunar surface.

Nuclear power matters because the lunar night lasts about two weeks, during which solar panels go dark and temperatures plunge. A reactor that runs through the darkness would let habitats, rovers, and science instruments operate continuously rather than hibernating. The call for partners is an early step, but it signals that surface nuclear power is moving from concept studies toward real hardware.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon

item.title: NASA awards $290.6 million contract for NOAA's next weather satellites
item.description:
NASA, acting on behalf of NOAA, has awarded Northrop Grumman a $290.6 million contract to build the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments for NOAA's Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The hybrid contract covers cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials work.

NEON is NOAA's next generation of polar-orbiting weather satellites, the spacecraft that feed the data behind everyday forecasts and severe-weather warnings. The microwave sounders measure temperature and moisture through the atmosphere, even under clouds, making them one of the most valuable inputs for forecast models. The award locks in a key piece of the program's hardware and keeps NEON on track to replace aging weather satellites.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program

item.title: Webb traces how supernova dust seeds new stars
item.description:
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has produced a detailed mid-infrared portrait of Cassiopeia A, the remnant of a massive star that exploded centuries ago. The high-resolution view maps the gas and dust thrown off by the blast — material that will eventually collapse into a new generation of stars and planets.

Supernova remnants like Cas A are the universe's recycling plants: the heavy elements forged inside a dying star get scattered into space, enriching the clouds that form future solar systems. Webb's observations let astronomers trace exactly how that dust is structured and how much of it survives the explosion, refining our understanding of how the raw ingredients of planets — and of us — get made and distributed.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA’s Webb Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles Star Evolution

item.title: Cancer research in microgravity could predict metastasis risk
item.description:
Aboard the International Space Station, the Encapsulate-1 investigation is growing patient-derived gastric microtumors inside a biochip to study how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. A November 19 image shows the tiny tumors taking shape in the experiment hardware.

Without gravity, cells behave differently — they cluster and migrate in ways that can reveal how tumors spread. The hope is that what researchers learn in orbit could lead to better tests for predicting a patient's risk of metastasis, and ultimately to more personalized cancer treatment. It's one of the clearest examples of the station doubling as a biomedical lab, using the space environment to ask questions that are hard to answer on Earth.

Sources

  • NASA: Studying Cancer Cells in Microgravity

item.title: New documentary follows Europa Clipper into deep space
item.description:
NASA has released a new documentary, "The Europa Concept," chronicling the Europa Clipper mission from a far-off vision to a spacecraft now cruising through deep space toward Jupiter's ice-covered moon. It premieres November 23 on NASA+, the NASA app, and the agency's website.

Europa is one of the most promising places in the solar system to look for life, with a global ocean hidden beneath its frozen shell. The film is a behind-the-scenes look at the people and engineering behind the mission, and it arrives while Clipper is still en route — a chance to catch up on the science and the stakes before the spacecraft reaches its destination and begins its close flybys.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space

item.title: Russia's routine ISS supply launch is suddenly a secret
item.description:
Russia is set to launch a routine cargo mission to the International Space Station tomorrow — and Roscosmos is treating it as if it were classified. When asked about the flight, NASA directed inquiries to Roscosmos, which declined to discuss it.

That silence is striking because ISS resupply flights are normally public, routine affairs, announced well in advance with cargo manifests and launch times. The secrecy invites speculation, especially on a day when reports also surfaced about a possible Russian nuclear-armed satellite. There is no evidence the two are connected, but the lack of transparency around an ordinary station delivery is unusual, and worth watching as the launch unfolds.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a big secret

item.title: NASA's Johnson Space Center marks 65 years of human spaceflight
item.description:
NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston has shaped human spaceflight for 65 years, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated the rendezvous and docking techniques Apollo needed, to the research aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years.

Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and missions for the next era — the Moon and, eventually, Mars — carrying forward the same center that trained every astronaut who has flown to the Moon. It's a quiet anniversary for a place whose work has been anything but quiet.

Sources

  • NASA: 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson

item.title: Juno captures Jupiter's swirls in vivid color
item.description:
Today's Astronomy Picture of the Day features Jupiter's clouds as seen by NASA's Juno spacecraft — a swirling canvas of bands, storms, and colors that still defies a complete explanation. Scientists still don't fully understand what creates the precise palette of the planet's clouds, a mix of chemistry, sunlight, and ferocious winds.

Juno has been orbiting Jupiter since 2016, and its close passes keep producing images that look more like abstract art than astronomy. This one is worth a click just to see it.

Sources

  • NASA: APOD: 2026 November 22 – Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno

item.title: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine draw a funding threat from Congress
item.description:
SpaceX's military satellite service Starshield is under scrutiny after changes made to the service in Ukraine in October 2026, and the incoming chair of the House committee overseeing it is now threatening SpaceX's funding. The dispute centers on what exactly changed and why — questions SpaceX is being pressed to answer in writing.

The stakes go beyond one contract: Starshield is the backbone of SpaceX's growing military business, and a funding fight in Congress could ripple into its broader Pentagon work. It's also the latest sign that SpaceX's dual role — commercial spaceflight giant and defense contractor entangled in an active war — keeps pulling it into political fights it can't easily fly above.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

item.title: SpaceX's lenders don't want their collateral launched into orbit
item.description:
SpaceX's bondholders want the company's valuable chip collateral kept on Earth and within reach — not launched into space, where it would be rather hard to repossess. The dispute highlights the strange new world of space finance: when your collateral is destined for orbit, traditional lending protections start to break down.

It's a real constraint on SpaceX's ambitions for space-based data centers. Lenders are happy to fund hardware they can seize if things go wrong; hardware circling the planet at 17,000 mph is a different proposition. How this gets resolved could set the template for financing the entire space data center industry.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space

item.title: NASA's new Moon plan is taking shape, but big questions remain
item.description:
NASA's revised plan for returning astronauts to the Moon is coming into focus, but key technical and programmatic questions are still being debated. The agency is working through architecture choices that will determine how — and how soon — crews get back to the lunar surface.

The debate matters because the Moon program has already been reshaped multiple times, and each revision carries schedule and cost consequences. For now, the plan exists in outline with the details still contested, which is a familiar place for Artemis-era planning — but the clock is ticking, and the longer the big questions stay open, the harder the timeline gets.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain

item.title: Rocket Report: a weekend of ups and downs, and Stoke hits an engine milestone
item.description:
This week's Rocket Report rounds up a mixed weekend in launch news, including Russia launching a Soyuz rocket carrying satellites intended to help enable drone attacks over Ukraine — a reminder that orbital launches remain entangled with the war. On the brighter side, Stoke Space celebrated a milestone for its engine program as it pushes toward a fully reusable rocket.

The weekly roundup remains the best single digest of an industry where the launch cadence keeps climbing and the line between commercial spaceflight and geopolitics keeps blurring. Stoke's progress is worth watching: a working reusable second stage would be a genuine step change, not just another incremental improvement.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

item.title: Curiosity photographs drifting twilight clouds and notches 49 drill samples
item.description:
NASA's Curiosity rover caught drifting twilight clouds over Gale Crater on October 31, its 5,061st Martian day. The rover uses its navigation cameras to capture the post-sunset clouds, which appear for only a short time each fall — a brief, beautiful window into Martian weather.

Meanwhile, a new collage shows all 49 drill holes Curiosity has made as of November 2026, each one a rock sample pulverized and analyzed by instruments inside the rover. Fourteen years into a mission planned for two, Curiosity is still doing real science: every sample adds to the picture of whether Mars was once habitable, and the clouds add a seasonal rhythm to a world that often looks frozen in time.

Sources

  • NASA: Curiosity Spots Drifting Twilight Clouds
  • NASA: NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover Collects Samples

item.title: NASA seeds 302 small-business projects with up to $171 million
item.description:
NASA's Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs have selected 302 projects for seed funding, totaling up to $171 million. The awards go to small businesses around the country working on technologies NASA needs for Moon and Mars exploration.

It's one of those quiet programs that punches above its weight: small firms get the capital to develop ideas that might otherwise die in a lab, and NASA gets a pipeline of technology it couldn't build in-house. The space economy angle matters too — the funding is explicitly meant to fuel US commercial space capability, not just NASA's own missions.

Sources

  • NASA: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation

item.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth
item.description:
Voyager 1, humanity's farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth — about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) — after more than 49 years of constant travel. The probe crossed the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) on November 18.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, and Voyager 1 is now the first human-made object to get that far from home. The milestone is a reminder of just how durable the 1977-era spacecraft has proven to be: it is still returning data from interstellar space nearly half a century after launch, operating on instruments and power systems designed long before most of today's spaceflight era began.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA's Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth

item.title: Google turns to Blue Origin for its space-based solar project
item.description:
Google is turning to Blue Origin for launch services for Project Suncatcher, its long-term moonshot to put solar power generation in space. The project envisions satellites collecting solar energy in orbit, where sunlight is uninterrupted, though it remains a far-future concept rather than a near-term product.

The deal is notable as a sign of Blue Origin's growing role as a launch provider for major tech customers, but Google's bigger challenge isn't the rocket — it's the underlying economics and engineering of beaming power from orbit at scale. Suncatcher remains an early-stage bet, and the launch partnership is one small step on a very long road.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains

item.title: NASA's new Moon plans create a problem for Orion
item.description:
NASA's revised approach to lunar landings is putting new demands on the Orion spacecraft, which was not originally designed to fly the profile the updated plans require. The changes are meant to make Moon landings easier overall, but they shift complexity onto Orion and its crew systems.

Agency officials are cautioning against moving too fast or cutting corners to meet the new architecture, emphasizing a responsibility to keep the program safe even as schedules tighten. The tension captures the central trade-off of the current Artemis reshaping: simplifying one part of the mission tends to complicate another, and Orion — the one piece that must carry astronauts home — is absorbing much of that burden.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

item.title: NASA test-fires RS-25 engine for future Artemis missions
item.description:
NASA fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 on November 18 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at Stennis Space Center in Mississippi, running the developmental engine for its planned full duration of 200 seconds. The test supports future Artemis missions that will rely on the RS-25, the Space Launch System's main engine.

The engine tested is a developmental unit that will not itself fly, but the hot-fire data feeds directly into the flight engines that will power upcoming Artemis launches. Steady progress on engine testing is one of the quieter but essential threads of the Artemis program: every successful long-duration firing de-risks the crewed missions that depend on the SLS stack performing exactly as designed.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Conducts Latest RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions

item.title: NASA data powers a way to find pulsars a million times faster
item.description:
Open data from NASA's Fermi mission helped an international team of scientists develop a method for finding pulsars about a million times faster than before. Pulsars — rapidly spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space — are valuable tools for studying extreme physics and testing general relativity, but the faint or unusual ones have been painstakingly hard to spot.

The breakthrough matters beyond a single catalog: faster pulsar discovery accelerates the search for gravitational-wave sources and deepens our map of the Milky Way's most extreme objects. It's also a win for open science — the result came not from a new telescope, but from researchers finding a smarter way to mine data NASA had already made freely available.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars

item.title: Voyager 1 passes one light-day from Earth, a first for any human-made object
item.description:
NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft passed one light-day away from Earth on November 17, 2026 — a distance no other human-made object has ever reached. To mark the milestone, the Empire State Building was illuminated in gold, a nod to the gold-plated copper phonograph record aboard the spacecraft: the Golden Record, carrying sounds and images of Earth into interstellar space.

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 has now been traveling for nearly half a century, and historians revisiting the Golden Record's creation say they are confident the record will last a very long time. The one-light-day mark is a reminder of just how far humanity's farthest emissary has gone — and how durable the message it carries may prove to be.

Sources

  • NASA: Empire State Building Goes Gold for Voyager
  • Space - Ars Technica: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details

item.title: ULA blames Vulcan failure on inadequate fuel supply to engines
item.description:
United Launch Alliance says the failure of its Vulcan rocket was caused by an inadequate fuel supply to the engines. The company has not yet detailed the full corrective plan, but the finding narrows the investigation to the propellant feed system rather than the engines themselves.

Vulcan is a linchpin of ULA's future — and of the US Space Force's launch plans — so the path back to flight matters well beyond one rocket. ULA remains, in NASA's words, a valued partner, and the focus now shifts to how quickly the fuel-supply issue can be fixed and the vehicle cleared to fly again.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says

item.title: NASA data clinches the first confirmed stellar merger of its kind
item.description:
Researchers have identified a first of its kind: a star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. The newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star has been nicknamed Bao, and the NASA-funded discovery was bolstered by quick-turn observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Stellar mergers have long been predicted but never before confirmed in this form, making Bao a landmark case for understanding how stars live, collide, and are reborn. The discovery also shows off Webb's ability to pivot fast to follow up on a tantalizing find — a capability that is becoming central to modern astronomy.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger

item.title: NASA sets November 29 for the next space station cargo launch
item.description:
NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST on Sunday, November 29, for the next cargo launch to the International Space Station. The Northrop Grumman Cygnus spacecraft will carry approximately 11,000 pounds of science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the orbiting laboratory, with a prelaunch media teleconference set for Monday, November 23.

The mission, CRS-25, keeps the station's steady resupply cadence going as the ISS continues its science program. Coverage plans are now set, and barring weather or technical delays, the launch will close out November with another delivery run to low Earth orbit.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Sets Coverage for Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Launch, Prelaunch

item.title: NASA challenges US companies to build better electric rocket engines
item.description:
NASA has launched a new competition inviting US companies to build prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters, a type of electric propulsion considered crucial for future space operations and exploration. Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions — the kind of steady, fuel-sipping push needed to move satellites and deep-space spacecraft.

The challenge is aimed at maturing a technology that sits between today's small satellite thrusters and the high-power systems future missions will need. For the companies competing, it is a chance to prove hardware that could end up powering everything from satellite constellations to crewed exploration.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies
